questions.stem: A water utility is commissioning new chemical dosing pumps at a treatment works. The manufacturer's engineer is on site for one day only, today, to set up and tune the pumps, and will not return under the contract. The maintenance technician who will look after the pumps for the next ten years has been rostered to a reservoir inspection forty minutes away. Commissioning starts in an hour. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the manufacturer's engineer to write up the tuning settings and adjustment steps in a commissioning report that can be handed to the technician afterwards.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes that what matters can be written down. A report records the final settings, not how the engineer decided on them or what to do when the water chemistry changes, which is what the technician will need in year three.

options.text: Attend the commissioning yourself, take detailed notes and photographs of each step, and brief the technician on everything at the next team meeting.
options.rationale: This puts a non-specialist between the expert and the eventual owner, so the technician receives a second-hand account filtered through someone who will never operate the pumps. The candidate confuses being present with being the right person present.

options.text: Arrange with the manufacturer for a paid return visit next month, when the technician's roster allows a full training day on the new pumps.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a scheduling clash as fixed and pays to recover an opportunity that is available today. The pumps would also run for a month with nobody trained to adjust them, which is the exposure the transfer exists to prevent.

options.text: Ask the maintenance supervisor to swap the technician's duty today so the technician can work alongside the engineer through the commissioning and tuning.
options.rationale: The engineer's presence is a one-day opportunity that will not recur. Getting the future owner beside the expert, handling the pumps while the tuning is done, transfers the judgement as well as the settings, and a routine inspection can be moved far more cheaply than this day can be recreated.

questions.explanation: When the person who holds knowledge is available only briefly, the transfer has to happen in that window, with the eventual owner present and doing the work. Written outputs and later visits are useful supplements, but they recover only what the expert thought to write down or is paid to come back for. A short-lived chance to learn first-hand outranks routine arrangements that can be moved.
questions.mindset: When the expert is in the room only once, get the future owner into the room.

questions.stem: Your consultancy is bidding to upgrade signalling on a regional rail line. The prospective client asks to see the full lessons-learned report from a similar project you delivered last year for a different rail operator. That report includes the operator's contract values, an account of a dispute with its subcontractor and the names of its staff. Your contract with that operator contains a standard confidentiality clause. How should you respond?

options.text: Offer a summary of the transferable lessons with the former client's identity, commercial figures and named individuals removed, and explain why the full report is withheld.
options.rationale: The lessons themselves are the firm's experience and can travel; the commercial facts and people they were drawn from belong to the former client. Separating the two gives the prospective client what it actually needs while honouring the obligation.

options.text: Send the full report, because the lessons belong to your consultancy and showing them openly is the strongest evidence of the experience you are selling.
options.rationale: The candidate treats ownership of the lessons as ownership of everything in the document. Contract values, a dispute and named staff are the former client's information, and releasing them breaches the clause whatever the commercial benefit.

options.text: Decline to share any lessons from that project, explaining that client confidentiality prevents the firm from discussing the content of earlier engagements with anyone.
options.rationale: This over-reads the clause. Confidentiality protects the client's information, not the general know-how the firm gained, so refusing everything throws away legitimate, reusable knowledge and weakens the bid for no reason.

options.text: Ask the former operator for written permission to release the full report as it stands, and hold that part of the bid response until their reply arrives.
options.rationale: The candidate seeks release of material the new client does not need, such as a dispute and named staff, and delays the bid while doing so. The request also puts the earlier relationship under strain when a sanitised summary would serve.

questions.explanation: Lessons learned are reusable organisational knowledge, but the facts they were drawn from may belong to someone else. Transferring them across a confidentiality boundary means separating the lesson — the condition, the cause and what to do differently — from the identifying and commercial detail it came wrapped in. Withholding everything wastes the knowledge; releasing everything breaches the obligation.
questions.mindset: Share the lesson, not the client's business.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is customising a CRM platform for a housing association, with go-live in seven weeks. The sponsor asks you to produce a knowledge transfer plan by Friday so it can be approved at the next board meeting. The project team disbands at go-live. Nobody has yet been named to own the configured platform afterwards; the IT director and the head of tenant services each assume the other will. What should you do?

options.text: Write the plan by Friday against a generic support role, setting out the documents, walkthrough sessions and system access that whoever takes ownership will receive.
options.rationale: The candidate meets the request as framed and produces a plan that describes what will be handed out but cannot say who will learn it or check that they have. The board would approve a plan that hides the real gap.

options.text: Tell the sponsor the plan cannot be meaningful until an owner is named, and ask for that decision to go to the board with the plan's outline attached.
options.rationale: A transfer plan is a plan for a particular receiver to learn particular things. Surfacing the missing owner to the person who can get it decided, and using the board meeting to decide it, turns a paper exercise into a transfer that can actually happen in seven weeks.

options.text: Draft the plan by Friday with the IT director's team as the assumed receiver, since platform support usually sits with IT, and adjust it later if needed.
options.rationale: This settles an ownership question that is not the project manager's to settle, on the strength of a convention. If tenant services ends up owning the business configuration, the transfer will have gone to the wrong people.

options.text: Ask the IT director and the head of tenant services to agree between them who will own the platform, and write the plan once they report back.
options.rationale: The two have already each assumed the other will own it, so asking them to resolve it as peers is likely to stall. The candidate routes an ownership decision sideways instead of to the sponsor and board who can make it.

questions.explanation: A transfer has a giver and a receiver, and a plan written without a named receiver can only describe what will be handed out, not what will be learned. When the receiving owner is undecided, the first task is to get that decision made by someone with the authority to make it, and to be clear that the transfer timeline runs from that decision. A request for a deliverable can carry a hidden premise that is worth surfacing before the work starts.
questions.mindset: Ask who is receiving the knowledge before planning how to hand it over.

questions.stem: At the end of the design phase of a hospital car-park extension, your lessons register has eleven entries. Typical ones read 'Communication with the structural engineer could have been better' and 'Planning permission took longer than expected'. The register goes to the PMO at the phase gate next week, where it is published for other projects to use. What should you do before submitting it?

options.text: Submit the register as it stands, since the PMO's reviewers and other project managers can follow up with you on any entry they find relevant to their own work later.
options.rationale: The candidate relies on the author staying available to explain the lessons. Vague entries do not tell a reader whether they are relevant, so nobody follows up, and the knowledge stays with this team.

options.text: Add a severity rating and a phase tag to each entry so that other project managers can filter the register and find the most significant items quickly.
options.rationale: Better indexing makes entries easier to find but no easier to act on. The candidate improves the register's structure while leaving every entry as unusable as before.

options.text: Rework each entry with the team to say what happened, why it happened and what a future project should do differently, naming who should act on it.
options.rationale: An entry becomes usable by someone else only when it carries the situation, the cause and a specific recommendation. Doing it with the team while the phase is fresh is the only time those details are still easy to recover.

options.text: Consolidate the eleven entries into three broad themes with a short summary for each, so the register is concise and other projects can take in the main points at a glance.
options.rationale: Merging vague entries into broader themes makes them vaguer still. The candidate optimises for brevity when the problem is the absence of causes and recommendations.

questions.explanation: A lesson is reusable only when a stranger can act on it: it needs the situation, the cause and a specific recommendation, not a verdict on how things felt. Indexing, condensing and offering to answer questions all leave the content as unusable as before. Test each entry by asking whether a project manager who never met the team would know what to do differently after reading it.
questions.mindset: Write each lesson for a stranger who must act on it.

questions.stem: On a pension administration migration, two senior analysts hold most of the knowledge of the legacy calculation rules. For three weeks you have asked them to pair with junior colleagues and annotate the rules. Both agree in meetings, then the pairing sessions are quietly cancelled for 'urgent' work. Their line manager supports the project. The migration's test phase starts in two months. What should you do next?

options.text: Ask their line manager to make the pairing sessions a formal objective for both analysts, with progress reviewed at their monthly one-to-ones.
options.rationale: The candidate escalates to compel behaviour before understanding it. If the analysts fear for their position, formal pressure confirms the fear and tends to produce compliance on paper rather than real sharing.

options.text: Make the annotated rules a tracked deliverable in the project plan with named owners and dates, and report its status at each weekly review.
options.rationale: Tracking makes the slippage visible but assumes the problem is one of priority. The candidate treats a behavioural signal as a scheduling issue, so the sessions may keep being cancelled, now with a red status attached.

options.text: Meet each analyst privately to find out what they expect to lose or risk by sharing the knowledge, before deciding how to change the arrangement.
options.rationale: Agreement followed by avoidance means something has not been said. The cause could be workload, job security, status or doubts about the juniors, and each calls for a different fix; asking first is what lets the next step address the real one.

options.text: Protect the pairing time by asking the operations lead to divert the analysts' urgent work to other staff for the next eight weeks.
options.rationale: The candidate accepts the stated reason at face value. If workload is the real cause this helps, but if it is not, the 'urgent' work will be replaced by another reason and the operations team will have been disrupted for nothing.

questions.explanation: When people agree to share knowledge and then do not, their behaviour is telling you something their words did not. The cause might be workload, job security, status, or doubt that the receivers are ready, and each calls for a different response. Escalating, scheduling or clearing time each assume one cause in advance; establishing the cause first is what makes the eventual intervention work.
questions.mindset: When agreement and behaviour diverge, find out why before pushing harder.

questions.stem: Your agile team building a booking platform for a chain of dental clinics uses a tool that transcribes every meeting and makes the transcripts searchable. At the retrospective, the team proposes dropping its lightweight decision log because 'everything is already in the transcripts'. Last month two developers lost a day of rework after each found a different transcript in which the same design question had been discussed. What should you do?

options.text: Point out that transcripts record what was said rather than what was decided, and propose keeping the log as a short record of each settled decision and its reason.
options.rationale: The rework last month is direct evidence of the gap: two transcripts, two readings, one decision. Naming the difference between a record of discussion and a record of outcome lets the team keep the log for the one job transcripts cannot do.

options.text: Accept the proposal, since the team owns its working practices, and suggest the team tags key decisions inside the transcripts so they can be found later.
options.rationale: Self-organisation is a real principle, but the candidate defers to it without sharing evidence the team has overlooked. Tagging transcripts still leaves readers to work out which discussion superseded which, so it rebuilds the log in a worse form.

options.text: Accept the proposal for a trial of three sprints, and review at a later retrospective whether rework caused by conflicting or reopened decisions has gone up or down.
options.rationale: Experimenting is sound when the outcome is unknown, but here the evidence already exists. The candidate runs a trial whose likely result the team has already paid for once.

options.text: Keep both the decision log and the transcripts, and ask the scrum master to reconcile the log against each meeting's transcript afterwards so that the two records stay consistent.
options.rationale: This keeps the log but adds a reconciliation chore without engaging the team's reasoning. The candidate overrides the proposal by adding process rather than addressing the misunderstanding behind it, so the proposal will return.

questions.explanation: Raw records and curated knowledge do different jobs. A transcript or recording preserves everything, including every option that was raised and dropped, so finding the current position means reading the history and guessing which discussion won. A decision record exists to state the outcome and its reason once, so anyone can find what stands without reinterpreting it. More capture is not the same as more transferable knowledge.
questions.mindset: Capturing everything is not the same as recording what was decided.

questions.stem: Your agile team owns an address-validation component used in an online insurance quote journey. A second team, building a claims portal, wants to reuse it and asks for your most senior developer for two weeks to explain how it works. Your team is midway through a release with a fixed regulatory date in five sprints, and that developer is working on the critical stories. What should you propose?

options.text: Ask your senior developer to record a detailed walkthrough of the component's design and code, and share it with the claims team along with the existing documentation.
options.rationale: The candidate picks the cheapest option for the giving team. A recording shows how the component looks but not how to change it safely, and the claims team's questions will come back to the senior developer anyway, one at a time.

options.text: Decline the request until after the regulatory release has shipped, and offer the claims team a full two-week session with the senior developer at that point instead.
options.rationale: This protects your date by putting the other team's work entirely on hold for five sprints. The candidate treats the choice as all-or-nothing when a smaller form of transfer could start now.

options.text: Agree to the two weeks, since reuse across teams benefits the organisation, and ask the product owner to move the senior developer's stories to later sprints.
options.rationale: The candidate values organisational reuse over a fixed regulatory commitment and removes a critical developer mid-release. Moving critical stories later compresses the sprints closest to an immovable date.

options.text: Invite one of the claims team's developers to join your team for a sprint and work on stories that touch the component, accepting a small dip in your velocity.
options.rationale: Embedding a learner inside the owning team transfers working knowledge through real changes while the experts keep delivering. The cost is a modest, bounded slowdown rather than the loss of a critical developer, which is a trade both teams can live with.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer between teams costs the giving team something, and the choice is about which form of the cost is affordable. Bringing a learner into the team that owns the knowledge usually transfers the most for the least disruption, because they learn by doing real work while the experts keep delivering. Recordings are cheap but shallow; lending an expert or deferring entirely each puts one team's goal wholly behind the other's.
questions.mindset: Bring the learner to where the work is, rather than taking the expert away from it.

questions.stem: A bank is rolling a new teller system out to 30 branches in six waves, using a rollout playbook baselined after a successful pilot. Wave 1 has just finished: three of its five branches hit a printer-driver conflict the pilot never met, costing each branch half a day of service. Wave 2 starts in eight days. The playbook is under configuration control. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the baselined playbook for the remaining waves, and brief the wave 2 support team on the printer issue so they can resolve it quickly if it recurs.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the baseline as something to protect rather than to improve. A verbal briefing helps wave 2 react faster, but waves 3 to 6 depend on someone remembering, and the branches still lose service before the fix is applied.

options.text: Hold a short wave review with the wave 1 branch leads and support team, and submit an amended playbook through configuration control before wave 2 starts.
options.rationale: The playbook is what every later wave works from, so changing it is how wave 1's lesson reaches waves 2 to 6. Eight days is enough for a short review and a controlled amendment, and using configuration control keeps the baseline trustworthy.

options.text: Pause the rollout after wave 1 until the printer conflict has been fully diagnosed, documented and tested, then resume with a revised schedule for all later waves.
options.rationale: The candidate responds to a contained, already-understood issue by stopping the programme. There are eight days to update the playbook before wave 2, so pausing costs schedule without buying anything the review would not.

options.text: Log the printer conflict in the lessons register for review at the end of the rollout, so that the full pattern across all six waves can be analysed together.
options.rationale: An end-of-rollout review is too late for the five waves that need the lesson. The candidate files the knowledge where it will be analysed rather than where it will be used.

questions.explanation: In a staged rollout, each stage is a source of knowledge for the next, and what carries that knowledge forward is the artefact the next stage works from. Updating that artefact between stages, through whatever control applies to it, is how a lesson changes what happens next. Lessons held only in people's memories, or saved for an end-of-programme review, arrive too late for the stages that needed them.
questions.mindset: Feed what each stage learned into the instructions for the next before it starts.

questions.stem: You manage the design of a ship's ballast-water treatment system. The pump-control subsystem, designed by one team, will be integrated by another team starting in six weeks. You want a two-day teach-back in which the integration team explains the design back to its designers, so gaps surface early. Both teams work for you within the approved plan, and the integration activity has eight days of float. What should you do?

options.text: Schedule the two-day teach-back within the existing float, update the schedule, and report the change to the steering group in your next status report.
options.rationale: Allocating team time within the approved plan and using available float are inside a project manager's delegated authority. Acting now secures the session while both teams are available, and reporting it keeps governance informed without asking it to decide.

options.text: Raise a change request for the steering group to approve the two days, since the teach-back session was not included in the approved baseline schedule.
options.rationale: The candidate reads every unplanned activity as a baseline change. Using float within the plan does not alter scope, cost or milestones, so a change request spends governance time on a decision the project manager already owns.

options.text: Ask the integration team to read the design documentation and submit written questions, so the designers can answer them without taking time away from the plan.
options.rationale: The candidate avoids spending time that is already available and settles for a weaker channel. Written questions reveal only the gaps the integrators know about, whereas explaining the design back exposes the ones they do not.

options.text: Wait until integration begins, and arrange for a designer to be available on call to answer the integration team's questions as they arise during the work.
options.rationale: On-call support helps, but it moves discovery of misunderstandings into the integration activity itself, where each one costs rework. The candidate defers a check that is cheapest before the work starts.

questions.explanation: A project manager uses delegated authority to organise work within the approved plan, and spending available float on an activity that protects the plan's outcome falls inside it. Escalating such decisions wastes governance attention and delays action, while settling for a cheaper channel to avoid a decision gives up the benefit. Know where your authority ends, and act fully inside it.
questions.mindset: Use the authority you already have before asking for more.

questions.stem: The sponsor has cancelled your logistics company's route-optimisation project at 60% complete because a merger has made it redundant. The eight team members are reassigned next Friday, and the PMO's closure checklist assumes a three-week closure with a full lessons workshop. The supplier evaluation and the requirements analysis are almost certainly reusable by the merged company's own planning project. With five working days left, what should you prioritise?

options.text: Ask the PMO for a three-week extension of the team's assignments so that the full closure checklist and lessons workshop can be completed as designed.
options.rationale: The candidate tries to restore the standard process instead of working within the decision already taken. Holding eight people on a cancelled project for three weeks is unlikely to be approved and spends days waiting for the answer.

options.text: Spend the remaining days packaging the supplier evaluation and requirements analysis with their reasoning and contacts, and hand them to the planning project's manager.
options.rationale: The cancellation and the reassignment date are fixed, so the remaining effort should go where it will be reused. Transferring the two valuable assets, with the reasoning behind them, directly to a known recipient gets the most value out of five days.

options.text: Run the full lessons workshop on the Monday, condensed into a single day, so that the team's reflections are captured before everyone disperses.
options.rationale: A compressed generic workshop produces thin output aimed at nobody in particular. The candidate follows the shape of the closure process when the time would buy more if spent on the two assets with a known reuser.

options.text: Archive all project documents in the repository with an index, so that any future project can find whatever material turns out to be relevant to it.
options.rationale: An archive without a recipient depends on someone thinking to look. The candidate opts for completeness over transfer, while the one project that certainly needs the material is not told it exists.

questions.explanation: When the time for closure is cut short, knowledge capture should be aimed at the material most likely to be reused and at the people most likely to reuse it. A complete, generic process run under compression produces thin outputs for nobody in particular, and an archive without a recipient is a store nobody visits. Direct transfer to a known next user beats comprehensive capture for an unknown one.
questions.mindset: With little time, transfer what will be reused to the people who will reuse it.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a consumer lending app. Eight months ago, a compliance officer told the product owner in a corridor conversation how a rule on affordability checks should be interpreted, and the team built three features on that reading. Nothing was written down. Internal audit has announced it will sample affordability decisions across all lending products next quarter, and the head of compliance is unaware of the interpretation. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the compliance officer to confirm the interpretation by email, and attach that email to the team's decision log as the evidence behind the three features.
options.rationale: This captures the knowledge in writing, which is a real improvement, but it records one individual's view rather than the function's position. Audit will test against what compliance holds on record, and if the head of compliance reads the rule differently the team will find out during the audit.

options.text: Write the interpretation up as an architecture decision record with the context and reasoning, and review it with the whole team at the next sprint review.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the problem as undocumented team knowledge. A decision record makes the team's understanding explicit, but it is still the team's record of someone else's ruling, and nobody in compliance has confirmed it.

options.text: Take the interpretation, as the team has applied it, to the head of compliance and ask the compliance function to confirm it and record it in its own register.
options.rationale: The interpretation is only as durable as the function that owns it. Having compliance confirm and record it moves the knowledge from one conversation into the organisation that will be answerable for it at audit, and surfaces any disagreement while the three features can still be adjusted.

options.text: Add the unconfirmed interpretation to the risk register, and ask the product owner to schedule a spike to assess the rework the three features would need if it changed.
options.rationale: Sizing the exposure is useful, but the candidate plans for the consequence before taking the cheaper step of getting the interpretation confirmed. With a quarter before the audit, the risk can be closed rather than merely measured.

questions.explanation: Some knowledge a project relies on belongs to a function outside the team — legal, compliance, safety, finance — and is authoritative only when that function holds it. When such knowledge exists only in one person's head or one conversation, the transfer that matters is to the owning function, which must confirm and record it, not to the team's own documents. A personal confirmation preserves the words but not the authority behind them.
questions.mindset: Move knowledge to the owner who must stand behind it, not just onto paper.

questions.stem: Your agile team has released the first increments of a new online billing portal for an energy supplier. The customer service team escalates around fifteen tickets a week to your developers, and most concern issues for which the developers already know a workaround. Those workarounds are scattered across the team's chat channel and in individual developers' heads. Customer service staff have no access to the channel. What should you do?

options.text: Give customer service team leads read access to the developers' chat channel, so they can search for workarounds there before deciding to escalate a ticket.
options.rationale: This grants access without making the knowledge usable. A busy development channel mixes workarounds with half-finished discussion, and customer service staff would have to judge which messages still hold.

options.text: Set up a daily developer rota for answering escalations, so tickets are handled quickly and the rest of the team can stay focused on the sprint goal.
options.rationale: The rota makes the team faster at answering the same questions repeatedly. The candidate optimises the response to escalations instead of removing the reason they happen.

options.text: Plan a full support manual for the portal as a backlog item before the final release, when the features will be stable enough to describe accurately.
options.rationale: The candidate waits for completeness while customers meet the issues now. Postponing the transfer until the end leaves fifteen escalations a week in place for the rest of the build.

options.text: Create a known-issues page with customer service, listing each issue and its workaround, and make keeping it current part of the team's definition of done.
options.rationale: The knowledge exists but sits where its users cannot see it. A shared page built with the people who use it, and maintained as part of finishing work, puts the workarounds in front of customer service before they need to escalate.

questions.explanation: Knowledge that exists inside a team is still unavailable to the people outside it unless it is put somewhere they can find and trust. The usual fix is a small, maintained artefact built with its users and kept up to date as part of normal work, rather than broader access to raw conversations or a comprehensive document at the end. Repeated questions are a sign that knowledge is invisible, not that answers are slow.
questions.mindset: When the same question keeps arriving, publish the answer where the askers can find it.

questions.stem: A contractor is completing a new hospital outpatient wing that the trust's estates team will operate and maintain for the next thirty years. The contract requires a handover package before practical completion. The estates manager has told you that on the last new building, his team spent its first year discovering how the ventilation and access-control systems actually worked. Which two arrangements should you insist on before accepting handover?

options.text: Estates engineers attend the witnessed commissioning tests and the contractor's system training, with attendance and any unresolved questions recorded.
options.rationale: Seeing the systems run and fail under test, with the installers present, is how the people who inherit them learn how they actually behave. Recording questions makes sure nothing is left hanging at the point the contractor leaves.

options.text: The as-built drawings and operation and maintenance manuals are checked against the installed plant by estates staff before acceptance.
options.rationale: Documents that describe the design rather than what was built are the classic cause of a year of discovery. Having the receiving team verify them on site turns a contractual deliverable into knowledge the estates team trusts.

options.text: The contractor provides a telephone helpline staffed by its engineers for the twelve-month defects liability period after handover.
options.rationale: A helpline is useful backup, but the candidate keeps the knowledge with the contractor and expires it after a year. The estates team still has to learn the systems, one call at a time.

options.text: The contractor's full site diaries and design-change log are included in the handover package for reference by the estates team.
options.rationale: The candidate equates more documents with more knowledge. Diaries and change logs hold the history of construction, but they do not tell an engineer how the building is meant to run.

options.text: The contractor operates the building on the trust's behalf for the first six months, with estates staff taking over once the systems have settled.
options.rationale: This defers the transfer instead of completing it and adds an operating contract the scenario has not justified. When the six months end, the estates team is in the same position it would have been at handover.

questions.explanation: Handover into operations transfers knowledge only when the receiving team can run what it receives. That requires the receivers to see the systems working with the people who installed them, and to confirm that the documentation describes what was actually built. Extra history, contractor support or delayed takeover each keep the knowledge with the supplier for longer rather than moving it.
questions.mindset: Accept a handover when the receivers can run it, not when the package is complete.

questions.stem: Your agile team of fourteen, building a logistics tracking product, has become too large to work well. You and the product owner agree to split it into two teams of seven, each owning part of the product, from the start of the next quarter. Five developers have built most of the shared data layer that both new teams will depend on. Which two actions best preserve the team's knowledge through the split?

options.text: Form the two teams so that each includes developers who have worked on the shared data layer, accepting that neither team is staffed entirely with its preferred specialists.
options.rationale: Spreading the people who know the shared layer across both teams keeps that knowledge where both teams need it. The cost is a less specialised split, which is the right trade for a dependency both teams share.

options.text: Set up a regular cross-team session for everyone working on the shared data layer, to review changes and agree conventions after the split takes effect.
options.rationale: A community of practice around the shared component keeps knowledge flowing between teams after the split. It costs a little time from each team but prevents two diverging understandings of the same code.

options.text: Place all five data-layer developers in one team that owns the shared layer, and have the other team raise requests to them for any changes it needs.
options.rationale: This keeps the experts together and is efficient in the short term, but it concentrates the knowledge in one team and makes the other dependent on it. The candidate chooses specialisation over spread when both teams need the layer.

options.text: Ask the five data-layer developers to write full documentation of the shared layer during the remaining sprints, before the two new teams are formed.
options.rationale: Documentation helps, but the candidate relies on it to carry knowledge that is mostly learned by changing the code. It also takes the five developers who know most away from delivery just before a disruptive change.

options.text: Keep a single combined backlog refinement session for all fourteen people, so everyone continues to hear about every item across the whole product.
options.rationale: The candidate tries to preserve shared knowledge by keeping the old team together in its most expensive meeting. This brings back the coordination overhead that the split was meant to remove.

questions.explanation: When a team splits, its knowledge goes with whichever people end up in each new team, so the composition decision is also a knowledge-distribution decision. Spreading people who know shared components, and creating a lightweight forum for those components afterwards, keeps understanding aligned without restoring the overhead the split removed. Concentrating expertise is efficient at first and creates dependency later.
questions.mindset: When a team divides, decide where the knowledge goes as deliberately as where the work goes.

questions.stem: An insurer's in-house team is taking over a claims-triage application built by a supplier under a hybrid contract. Knowledge transfer is a contract milestone that triggers a €120,000 payment. The supplier proposes that the milestone be accepted once 40 hours of training have been delivered and the documentation set has been signed off. Which two acceptance criteria would better show that the transfer has worked?

options.text: The insurer's developers make a planned change and release it to production themselves, with the supplier observing but not intervening.
options.rationale: Delivering a real change without help tests the whole chain of knowledge — code, build, test and release. It measures what the insurer can now do rather than what it has been shown.

options.text: The insurer's support staff resolve a simulated production incident within the agreed service level, using only the runbooks and their own knowledge.
options.rationale: An incident under time pressure is where gaps in operational knowledge show. Passing it with the runbooks alone shows that the documentation and the people together can run the service.

options.text: The training hours are increased to 80 and the sessions are recorded, so the insurer's staff can return to them after the supplier leaves.
options.rationale: The candidate keeps the supplier's input measure and simply raises the quantity. More training delivered still says nothing about whether the insurer's team can do the work.

options.text: Every member of the in-house team completes a satisfaction survey rating the training and documentation as good or better before payment.
options.rationale: Satisfaction measures how the transfer felt, not what it achieved. People often rate clear training highly and still cannot operate the system alone.

options.text: The documentation set is reviewed by the insurer's architect for completeness against an agreed index of topics before sign-off.
options.rationale: A completeness review improves the documents, but it is still an input check. The candidate accepts the supplier's premise that a full set of materials equals transferred capability.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer is complete when the receivers can do the work without the givers, so acceptance should rest on demonstrated performance rather than on what was delivered to them. Training hours, document sign-off and satisfaction ratings measure effort and impressions, not capability. Where payment depends on transfer, the criterion should be a task the receiving team performs unaided under realistic conditions.
questions.mindset: Measure a transfer by what the receivers can now do, not by what they were given.

questions.stem: Your agile team at a ticketing company has three knowledge needs this quarter. Match each need to the method that suits the kind of knowledge involved. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A new developer must learn the stable, scripted twelve-step routine for deploying the ticketing service to production.
A junior analyst must learn how the senior analyst judges which customer complaints point to a deeper product defect.
Developers joining next year will need to know why the team chose an event-driven design eighteen months ago.

options.text: A maintained runbook or checklist
options.rationale: A stable, repeatable procedure is explicit knowledge. Writing it down once, and keeping it current, transfers it to anyone who follows the steps.

options.text: Shadowing and pairing on live cases
options.rationale: Judgement about which complaints matter is tacit knowledge built from experience. It transfers by working through real cases alongside the person who has it.

options.text: A decision record with context and reasoning
options.rationale: The people who will need this have not joined yet. A short record of the decision, the options considered and the reasons is the only way to reach a reader who is not yet on the team.

options.text: A recorded all-hands presentation
options.rationale: Not used. A one-off broadcast can raise awareness, but it suits none of these needs: it is too general for a procedure, too passive for judgement, and too hard to find later for a design rationale.

questions.explanation: The method of transfer should follow the kind of knowledge being moved. Explicit, stable procedures travel well in written form; tacit judgement travels through shared work on real cases; and the reasoning behind past decisions must be recorded for readers who are not yet present. Using one method for all knowledge leaves some of it untransferred.
questions.mindset: Choose how to transfer knowledge by first asking what kind of knowledge it is.

questions.stem: A construction firm's PMO reviews why its lessons-learned process is not working. Match each symptom it found to the most likely cause. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Registers hold almost no lessons about estimating errors or design mistakes, although post-project audits show both were common.
The same ground-survey lesson has been recorded on six projects in four years, each time with the same recommendation.
Lessons from the firm's rail depot projects are never applied on its hospital projects, although both report the same problems with utility diversions.

options.text: Recording a mistake is seen as admitting fault, so people leave out lessons that reflect on themselves or colleagues
options.rationale: When the missing lessons are specifically the ones about errors, the filter is what people are willing to admit, not what they can remember. Capture has to be framed around conditions and causes rather than culprits before those lessons will appear.

options.text: No one owns turning recommendations into changes to the standard processes and templates every project starts from
options.rationale: When a lesson recurs with the same recommendation, the recommendation is being written but not implemented. Someone has to own changing the standard so the next project starts from the corrected version.

options.text: Lessons are filed and circulated only within the sector division that produced them, so other divisions never see them
options.rationale: A shared problem that is solved in one division and repeated in another shows that lessons travel only along organisational lines. They need to be classified by the activity or risk they concern, so a utility-diversion lesson reaches anyone planning one.

options.text: Capture happens long after events, at project close, when the details and causes have faded from memory
options.rationale: Not used. Late capture thins out every lesson, but it would not selectively remove the ones about mistakes while keeping the rest, and it explains neither a recurring recommendation nor a lesson that never crosses divisions.

questions.explanation: A lessons process can fail at capture, at action or at distribution, and each failure leaves a different trace. Lessons missing in a pattern point to what people feel safe recording; a lesson that keeps recurring points to recommendations nobody is responsible for implementing; a lesson that stays inside one part of the organisation points to how lessons are classified and circulated. Fixing the wrong stage leaves the process failing.
questions.mindset: Find where the lesson stops travelling before deciding how to fix the process.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme for a regional airport identifies lessons at the end of each iteration and each stage. Complete each sentence with the action that sends the lesson to whoever can act on it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A lesson shows that the organisation's standard estimating template understates testing effort for every project. The project manager should
A lesson shows that the team's handoffs to the baggage-systems supplier lose detail within this programme. The team should

options.text: submit it to the PMO, which owns the template, with the evidence and a proposed amendment
options.rationale: The template is an organisational asset that the project does not own. Routing the lesson to its owner, with evidence, is how the correction reaches every future project rather than only this one.

options.text: agree a change to its own handoff practice at the next iteration planning and apply it straight away
options.rationale: The lesson concerns a practice the team controls and still has to use. Acting on it in the next iteration means the remaining work benefits, without waiting for anyone else's approval.

options.text: record it in the lessons register for discussion at the programme's final closure review
options.rationale: Not used. Holding either lesson for closure delays its use: the template stays wrong for every project in the meantime, and the handoff problem continues for the rest of the programme.

questions.explanation: A lesson should go to whoever owns the thing that needs to change. When it concerns an organisational standard, the owner of that standard must amend it; when it concerns the team's own practice, the team should change it at the next opportunity. Recording lessons without routing them is how the same lesson ends up being learned again.
questions.mindset: Send each lesson to the owner of whatever has to change.

questions.stem: A laboratory instrument-validation project relies on 15 critical procedures. A skills matrix shows that 6 of them can be performed by only one person. The target is for every procedure to have at least two capable people. Transferring one procedure takes a 3-hour pairing session involving the expert and one learner.

blanks.label: Percentage of critical procedures with only one capable person
blanks.rationale: 6 ÷ 15 = 0.40, so 40% of the critical procedures depend on a single person. Putting that figure in front of the sponsor makes the exposure visible in a way a general warning does not.

blanks.label: Total person-hours needed to bring every procedure to two capable people
blanks.rationale: Each of the 6 procedures needs one 3-hour session with two people present: 6 × 3 × 2 = 36 person-hours. Counting both the expert's and the learner's time gives the true cost of the transfer.

questions.explanation: Quantifying knowledge concentration turns a vague concern into a planning figure that can be weighed against other work. A skills matrix gives the share of critical capability held by one person, and the transfer effort is the number of gaps multiplied by session length and the number of people in each session. Counting only the learner's time understates the cost, because the expert's hours come out of delivery too.
questions.mindset: Put a number on knowledge risk so it can be planned for like any other work.

questions.stem: In sprint 9 your agile team lost two days because a shared test database was refreshed without warning. The team wants to agree a change to its own way of working so the lesson sticks. The diagram shows the team's regular events. Select the event designed for this.

graphic.title: The team's recurring events arranged around a two-week sprint
graphic.caption: Select an event. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between events, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Sprint planning — choose the work for the coming sprint
regions.rationale: Planning decides which backlog items to take on next. A team might mention the outage here, but the event is focused on the product work, not on how the team works.

regions.label: Daily scrum — inspect progress toward the sprint goal
regions.rationale: The daily scrum is a short check on progress and blockers. It could have flagged the outage on the day, but it is too brief for agreeing a lasting change to practice.

regions.label: Backlog refinement — clarify and size upcoming items
regions.rationale: Refinement prepares future product work. Choosing it treats a process lesson as a backlog item, which can work for tooling but leaves the team's working agreement unchanged.

regions.label: Sprint review — inspect the increment with stakeholders
regions.rationale: The review looks at the product with stakeholders. It is about what was built rather than how the team works, so it is the wrong forum for a change to practice.

regions.label: Sprint retrospective — inspect and improve how the team works
regions.rationale: The retrospective is where the team examines its own process and agrees changes to it. Turning the outage into an agreed practice here is how an agile team transfers a lesson into its future work.

questions.explanation: In an agile team, lessons about how the team works are captured and acted on at the retrospective, sprint by sprint, rather than saved for the end of the project. The other events inspect the product, the plan or daily progress. Matching the lesson to the event built for it is what turns a bad week into a lasting change.
questions.mindset: Turn each sprint's lessons into changes the team makes in the very next sprint.

questions.stem: You are being moved to a larger programme and will hand your county council's road-widening scheme to a new project manager in three weeks. The schedule, risk register and contracts are up to date. Over eighteen months you have also made several verbal agreements: weekend working limits with a residents' group, access arrangements with a garden centre owner, and an understanding with the utilities firm about diversion dates. What should you prioritise in the handover?

options.text: Spend most of the three weeks walking your successor through the schedule, risk register and contracts in detail, since these formal records will govern the remaining delivery work.
options.rationale: The candidate spends the scarce overlap on the knowledge that is least at risk. A competent successor can read up-to-date records alone; what cannot be read anywhere are the commitments that were never written down.

options.text: Prepare a comprehensive handover report covering the scheme's history, status and stakeholder background, and offer to answer your successor's questions by phone after you move.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes a document written alone transfers an agreement. The report records only your version of each understanding, the other parties never confirm it, and the phone offer leaves the successor dependent on your goodwill once you are busy elsewhere.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to delay your move until the utility diversions are complete, so that the agreements are honoured by the person who made them and nothing is lost in transition.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the knowledge as something only you can hold, which postpones the transfer rather than doing it. The agreements will outlast the diversions, and a delayed move simply moves the same handover problem to a later date.

options.text: Write each verbal agreement into the stakeholder and issue records, then introduce your successor to each party in person to confirm the agreement is understood the same way.
options.rationale: The formal records will transfer themselves; the agreements exist only in your memory and in three relationships. Recording them turns a personal understanding into a project obligation, and confirming them face to face with the successor present catches any difference in how each party remembers them.

questions.explanation: In any handover the formal records largely transfer themselves; the knowledge at risk is whatever lives only in the outgoing person's memory and relationships, such as informal commitments to stakeholders. Making those commitments explicit in the project's records and confirming them with the other party, with the successor present, converts a personal understanding into a project obligation that survives a change of people.
questions.mindset: Hand over what nobody wrote down before polishing what everyone can already read.

questions.stem: In the round-the-clock support period after a hospital's new pharmacy system went live, the overnight analyst found the interface to the dispensing robots switched off and assumed it had failed. The day team had switched it off on purpose while correcting drug codes, and restarting it sent forty duplicate orders to the robots. Handover between support shifts is a free-text note left in the ticket queue. The next shift change is at 20:00 today. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Introduce from tonight a live handover call, in which the outgoing analyst walks the incoming analyst through a standard checklist of disabled interfaces, temporary fixes and open incidents.
options.rationale: The failure was in the handover itself, and the next one is hours away. A two-way walk-through against a fixed list of system conditions lets the incoming analyst ask questions and makes it hard to omit a deliberate switch-off, which a one-way note cannot do.

options.text: Commission a formal post-incident review of the duplicate orders, and introduce new handover arrangements once its findings and recommendations have been reviewed and approved by the go-live manager.
options.rationale: The candidate waits for a process that will take days to reach a conclusion the facts already show. Several shift changes will pass under the same arrangement in the meantime, each able to repeat the incident.

options.text: Remind every support analyst that the ticket notes must be read in full at the start of each shift, and ask the day team to write far more detailed notes about anything they switch off.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the failure as a lapse of diligence and keeps the one-way written channel that has just failed. A longer note still gives the reader no chance to ask why an interface is off.

options.text: Arrange refresher training for the overnight analyst on the interface procedures, so that he recognises a deliberate switch-off for what it is on future shifts and responds to it correctly.
options.rationale: The candidate diagnoses a competence gap where there was an information gap. The overnight analyst knew the procedures; what he lacked was the current state of the system, which only the day team held.

questions.explanation: Where work passes between shifts or crews, knowledge of the current state of the work is perishable and has to move at the boundary in a form the receiver can question. A structured, two-way handover against a standard list of conditions closes the gaps a one-way written note leaves open, and a known failure in that handover is fixed before the next boundary rather than after an investigation.
questions.mindset: Fix a broken handover before the next handover, not after the next incident.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is transferring a tablet-coating process from development to a manufacturing site. A senior formulation scientist runs weekly sessions to teach two process engineers how she adjusts spray rates when coating defects appear. After five sessions the engineers say the sessions are hard to follow; she says they lack the basic chemistry. Technology transfer batches start in ten weeks, and she is keen to help. What should you do next?

options.text: Enrol the scientist on a short course in coaching and presentation skills, so that her remaining sessions become clearer and better structured for the engineers before the transfer batches.
options.rationale: The candidate accepts the engineers' account without testing it. If the real gap is in the engineers' foundations or in the content, a generic skills course spends weeks of a ten-week window on the wrong cause.

options.text: Book the two engineers onto a foundation module in pharmaceutical chemistry, so that they arrive at her remaining sessions with the background knowledge she expects them to have.
options.rationale: The candidate makes the mirror-image error and accepts the scientist's account without testing it. The engineers may have enough chemistry and still be unable to follow judgement that is never made explicit.

options.text: Sit in on the next session, then ask each engineer to explain back how they would respond to a specific coating defect, to find where the understanding breaks down.
options.rationale: Each side's explanation is a hypothesis. Watching the session and testing what the engineers can actually do with it shows whether the gap lies in her method, in the content or in their foundations, and only then is the right remedy obvious.

options.text: Ask the scientist to set out her adjustment rules in a written decision guide for each defect, which the engineers can then study at their own pace before the batches begin.
options.rationale: The candidate changes the medium without knowing what failed. Adjustments that rest on her judgement are hard to reduce to rules, so the guide may reproduce the same gap on paper.

questions.explanation: When a knowledge transfer stalls and the giver and the receivers blame each other, each account is a hypothesis rather than a finding. Observing the transfer and testing what the receivers can actually do locates the gap — in the method, the content or the receivers' starting knowledge — and the remedy follows from that. Choosing a fix on one party's word spends the remaining time on a cause that may not exist.
questions.mindset: When a transfer stalls, find where it breaks before deciding whose side to fix.

questions.stem: Your university library refurbishment finished six weeks late. Your draft lessons report records that the steering committee took seven weeks to choose between two shelving designs, during which the joinery contractor stood down. The sponsor, who chairs that committee, asks you to delete the lesson before the report goes to the estates PMO, saying it reads as an attack on her colleagues and will help nobody. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the lesson as she asks, because the sponsor owns the project's outputs and the report's main value lies in the many technical lessons that still remain in it.
options.rationale: The candidate treats sponsor authority as settling what the organisation learns. The biggest single cause of delay disappears from the record, so the next project that needs a design decision will meet the same wait.

options.text: Keep the lesson exactly as drafted and send the report to the PMO with a note of the sponsor's objection, so that the record stays complete and is not altered under pressure.
options.rationale: The candidate confuses accuracy with wording. A lesson framed as a verdict on a committee invites defence rather than action, and sending it over the sponsor's objection damages the relationship without making the lesson more useful.

options.text: Take the lesson out of the report but pass it privately to the head of the estates PMO, so that the people who plan future projects still learn of it without causing embarrassment.
options.rationale: The candidate creates a hidden channel. The lesson becomes unsearchable for anyone not in that conversation, and quietly working around the sponsor costs trust that the project will need again.

options.text: Rewrite the lesson around the decision process rather than the committee, stating the lead time a design choice needed and recommending decision deadlines in future schedules, and agree the wording with her.
options.rationale: Her objection is to the framing, not the facts. Describing the process and its cost keeps everything future projects need, gives them a concrete recommendation, and removes the reason to suppress it.

questions.explanation: A lesson is useful when it describes what happened in a process and what to do differently, and it tends to be resisted when it reads as a verdict on people. When a stakeholder objects to a lesson, the first question is whether the objection is to its substance or to its framing. Reframing around the process usually keeps the substance while removing the motive to suppress it; deleting or hiding it loses exactly the cause future projects most need to know.
questions.mindset: Write lessons about how decisions were made, not who made them, so that they survive being read.

questions.stem: You are planning installation of a bottling line from a German supplier. The lessons register of a sister plant that bought from the same supplier two years ago recommends doubling the factory acceptance test from five to ten days, after repeated software faults. Since then the supplier has moved testing to a new facility and replaced its controls engineering lead. Ten days of testing would push commissioning into the peak season. What should you do?

options.text: Speak to the sister plant's project manager to understand what caused the faults, then check with the supplier which of those causes still exist before you decide the test duration.
options.rationale: The recommendation is only as good as its cause. Learning the cause from the people who lived it, then testing whether it survives the supplier's changes, lets you size the test to the actual risk rather than to the old answer or an assumption.

options.text: Plan the ten-day test as the lesson recommends, and ask the supplier to keep its software engineers available for the whole period so that any faults found are cleared quickly.
options.rationale: The candidate applies the lesson without checking whether its cause still exists. If the faults came from conditions the supplier has since changed, five extra days are spent guarding against nothing, and commissioning lands in peak season for no gain.

options.text: Keep the standard five-day test, and add a contract clause requiring the supplier to correct, at its own cost and within agreed response times, any software faults that appear during commissioning.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the supplier's changes removed the cause, which nobody has tested. A new facility and a new lead can equally introduce problems, and a cost clause does not give back the production days lost to faults in peak season.

options.text: Ask the supplier for fault records from recent acceptance tests at its new facility, and set the duration of your test according to the fault rate those records show.
options.rationale: This is close, and data-driven, but it relies on the supplier's account alone and skips the people who know why the faults occurred. Without the original cause, a low recent fault rate may say nothing about the risk to your configuration.

questions.explanation: A lesson from another project is a conclusion drawn under particular conditions, and its recommendation holds only while its cause does. Before adopting or discarding it, establish what caused the original problem — usually from the people who experienced it — and check whether that cause is present in the new situation. A change of context can remove a cause or create a new one, so neither blind adoption nor confident dismissal is safe.
questions.mindset: Import the cause behind a lesson, not just its recommendation.

questions.stem: A local authority is replacing its 20-year-old housing benefit system using a hybrid approach. In requirements interviews, assessors describe the official process clearly. A supervisor then mentions that experienced staff keep a shared spreadsheet to catch overpayments the old system misses, and use certain screens in an unofficial order to avoid a known crash. Nobody mentioned either in the interviews. What should the project manager arrange next?

options.text: A second round of interviews with the assessors, asking them directly to list every workaround, spreadsheet and unofficial practice they use in their daily work.
options.rationale: The candidate expects people to recall what they no longer notice. Habitual workarounds feel like part of the job rather than separate steps, so asking harder produces much the same answers as the first round.

options.text: A structured questionnaire to all assessors about how they use each screen and report, so that every member of staff can contribute rather than only those interviewed.
options.rationale: The candidate widens the reach but keeps the same weakness. A questionnaire still depends on people describing their work from memory, which is exactly what failed to surface the workarounds.

options.text: A decision to treat the workarounds as defects of the old system that the new one will remove, keeping requirements based on the official process staff described.
options.rationale: The candidate dismisses the workarounds as noise. The spreadsheet performs a real control, catching overpayments, and leaving it out would lose a requirement the new system genuinely needs.

options.text: Analysts sitting with assessors while they process real claims, recording the workarounds and informal tools they use alongside the official steps.
options.rationale: Knowledge embedded in how people work shows itself when they are doing the work. Watching real claims being processed reveals the spreadsheet, the screen order and anything else nobody thought to describe.

questions.explanation: Much of what experienced staff know is embedded in how they do the work and is not reported when they are asked to describe it, because it no longer feels like a separate step. Observing the work as it happens surfaces the workarounds, informal tools and checks that often carry real business value. Knowledge that people cannot readily articulate has to be captured where it is used.
questions.mindset: Watch the work being done to find what nobody thinks to say.

questions.stem: Your company is building a ticketing and membership app for a museum group under a fixed-price contract that excludes training and knowledge transfer. Two sprints before the final release, the museum's digital manager asks your developers to spend time 'informally' teaching her two in-house developers the codebase so they can support it later. Your developers are willing but fully allocated to release work. What should you do?

options.text: Let your developers teach the museum's staff in short sessions alongside release work, since a client able to support the app is good for the relationship and for future work.
options.rationale: The candidate absorbs unplanned scope into a fully allocated team two sprints from release. The release is put at risk, the teaching is squeezed into whatever time is left, and the client learns that excluded work can be had for free.

options.text: Decline the request politely, explaining that knowledge transfer is excluded from the contract and that your team's commitment is to deliver the final release on time.
options.rationale: The candidate reads the contract correctly but treats the exclusion as the end of the matter. The museum has a real need, and refusing it outright leaves its in-house team unable to support the product it is paying for.

options.text: Welcome the request, estimate the effort it needs, and take it to the museum's contract sponsor and your account director to agree it as a scoped, priced change.
options.rationale: Knowledge transfer is real work with a cost and a schedule impact. Those who own the contract on each side can decide whether it is worth funding and when it should happen, so the transfer is planned rather than squeezed in.

options.text: Invite the museum's two developers to your team's sprint reviews and give them read access to the repository, so they learn the codebase without taking your developers' time.
options.rationale: The candidate hopes exposure will substitute for transfer. Sprint reviews show features rather than internals, and reading an unfamiliar repository without guidance rarely produces people able to support it.

questions.explanation: Knowledge transfer consumes the time of the people who hold the knowledge and has to be planned like any other deliverable. When a request for it falls outside the agreed scope, the decision belongs to those who own the contract on both sides, who can weigh its value against cost and schedule. Quietly absorbing it, or refusing it outright, leaves that decision with people who do not own it.
questions.mindset: Treat a request to share knowledge as real work that someone with authority must decide to fund.

questions.stem: Your UK team is handing a new warehouse control system to the client's operations staff at a distribution centre near Valencia. Training was delivered in English with printed manuals, and the operators passed the written quiz. In the first week of parallel running they made repeated errors in exception handling, and their supervisor says most of them only partly followed the sessions. You hold €40,000 of contingency for transition risks. What should you do?

options.text: Raise the language gap with the client's operations director as an issue for the client to resolve, since the skills of its own operators are the client's responsibility.
options.rationale: The candidate pushes back a transition risk the project was funded to carry. Successful handover is the project's deliverable, and waiting for the client to act leaves operators making errors on live work in the meantime.

options.text: Use the contingency to have the exception procedures translated and to run hands-on sessions in Spanish at the workstations, led by a bilingual trainer with the operators' supervisor.
options.rationale: The gap is in the medium, not the content. Delivering the knowledge in the operators' language, on the equipment they use, addresses the actual barrier, and the contingency exists for exactly this kind of transition risk.

options.text: Extend parallel running by four weeks so that the operators learn exception handling on live work, with your English-speaking team on hand to correct mistakes as they happen.
options.rationale: The candidate buys more time through the same channel that failed. Corrections given in a language the operators only partly follow will be partly understood, and four weeks of dual running is expensive for both sides.

options.text: Repeat the English training at a slower pace with extra worked exercises, and add a practical test so that only operators who pass it are allowed to process exceptions on the new system.
options.rationale: The practical test is a good idea, but the candidate repeats the transfer in the medium that caused the problem. Restricting exceptions to those who pass also leaves the centre short of capacity.

questions.explanation: A transfer is complete when the receivers can do the work, and a quiz passed in a second language can hide the fact that they cannot. Where the gap lies in the medium — language, format or setting — the remedy is to adapt the transfer to the receivers rather than to repeat it. When the project holds contingency for this kind of transition risk, the project manager can commit it without waiting for someone else to decide.
questions.mindset: Adapt the transfer to the people receiving it, using the authority you already hold.

questions.stem: Your agile team at an energy-trading firm started mob programming three sprints ago because only one developer understood the trade-settlement engine. Four of the six developers can now change it safely, but completed stories per sprint have fallen by about 30%. The product owner, facing a quarter-end regulatory deadline, asks the team to stop mobbing and return to working individually. What should you do?

options.text: Agree to stop mobbing until the quarter-end deadline has passed, then restart it afterwards so that the remaining two developers can also learn the settlement engine.
options.rationale: The candidate protects throughput now and defers the transfer to a later that seldom arrives. A regulatory deadline is also exactly when dependence on a few people is most dangerous.

options.text: Continue mobbing on all work and show the product owner how far the risk has fallen, since four people can now change the engine where previously only one could.
options.rationale: The candidate is right that the gain is real but treats the deadline as the product owner's problem. Applying the most expensive practice to routine work as well ignores a legitimate constraint.

options.text: Propose mobbing only on settlement-engine work and other areas held by one person, with routine stories returning to individual or paired work, and review the balance at the next retrospective.
options.rationale: This keeps the transfer where knowledge is concentrated and the work is risky, and releases capacity everywhere else. Reviewing it at the retrospective lets the team adjust the balance once the deadline pressure is clearer.

options.text: Ask the team to decide at its next retrospective whether to continue mobbing, since how the team works is its own decision and the product owner should not dictate its engineering practices.
options.rationale: The candidate is right that the team owns its practices, but uses that to sidestep the product owner's legitimate concern about outcomes. Deferring the question for a sprint resolves nothing in the meantime.

questions.explanation: Spreading knowledge costs delivery capacity, and the cost is worth paying where knowledge is concentrated and the work is risky, not everywhere. The useful response to pressure on throughput is to aim the transfer practice at the areas of highest concentration, release the rest, and inspect the result. Treating the choice as all or nothing either throws away the gain or ignores a real deadline.
questions.mindset: Spend knowledge-sharing effort where concentration is risky, not evenly across all work.

questions.stem: A developer who joined your agile team at a travel booking start-up two weeks ago has found nine steps in the onboarding guide that are wrong or missing, mostly about setting up the local environment. At the daily scrum, the team suggests that the most senior developer rewrites the guide next sprint, because she knows the set-up best. What should you suggest instead?

options.text: The senior developer rewrites the guide next sprint as proposed, using the new developer's list of nine problems as a checklist of what must be fixed first and in what order.
options.rationale: The candidate trusts expertise to produce a guide for beginners. The expert's familiarity is why the guide drifted: she cannot see which steps she performs without thinking, and her time is the team's scarcest.

options.text: The new developer corrects the guide as he works through it, with the senior developer reviewing his changes, since he can see which steps an unfamiliar reader finds unclear.
options.rationale: The newest reader is the best test of an onboarding guide, and correcting it as he goes costs very little. The senior review keeps it accurate without making her the author of something she cannot see from a beginner's side.

options.text: The team replaces the written guide with a recorded walkthrough of the set-up by the senior developer, which is quicker to make and easier for new joiners to follow.
options.rationale: The candidate changes the medium but keeps the same author's blind spots. A recording is also harder to correct than text, so it goes out of date sooner and stays wrong for longer.

options.text: The team adds a story to rewrite the guide properly and asks the product owner to prioritise it against the product work planned for the coming sprints.
options.rationale: The candidate makes upkeep of the guide compete with features, where it usually loses. The next joiner is likely to meet the same nine errors while the story waits in the backlog.

questions.explanation: Onboarding material is best tested and maintained by the people it is written for, because experts cannot see the steps they perform without thinking. Having each newcomer correct the material as they use it, with an expert checking accuracy, keeps it current at almost no extra cost. Knowledge assets decay when only their authors maintain them.
questions.mindset: Let the newest reader fix the guide, because only they can see its gaps.

questions.stem: Your agile team maintains an appointment-booking API used by twelve partner veterinary practices. Partners regularly raise support tickets after a release because the API reference still describes the old behaviour; it is updated by whoever has spare time, usually weeks later. At the retrospective, the team proposes a dedicated documentation sprint each quarter to bring the reference up to date. What should you suggest?

options.text: Accept the quarterly documentation sprint, and ask the product owner to schedule the first one as soon as possible so that the backlog of outdated reference pages is cleared.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the backlog as the problem rather than the habit that created it. Between documentation sprints the reference drifts again, so partners keep meeting undocumented behaviour for up to three months at a time.

options.text: Add 'API reference updated and reviewed' to the team's definition of done, so that no change to the API counts as finished until its documentation describes it.
options.rationale: Making the update part of finishing the change closes the gap between what the API does and what partners are told it does. The knowledge is written by the person who has just made the change, while it is fresh, and the reference is never more than one change behind.

options.text: Name one developer as owner of the API reference, updating it after each sprint review, so that a single person keeps it consistent while the rest of the team stays on product work.
options.rationale: The candidate fixes accountability but separates the writing from the knowing. One person documenting other people's changes after the event works from second-hand understanding, and the team gains a new single point of knowledge.

options.text: Generate the API reference automatically from annotations in the code, so that it is rebuilt on every build and the team no longer has to write or maintain reference pages by hand.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes generation removes the need for discipline. Generated pages list signatures but not the changes in behaviour, deprecations and migration notes partners need, and the annotations go stale in exactly the same way unless updating them is part of the work.
