questions.explanation: Documentation that describes a product stays accurate when updating it is part of completing the change that alters the product, not a separate task done later. Batching the upkeep guarantees a period in which the record is wrong, and handing it to someone other than the person who made the change loses detail. In agile teams the definition of done is the mechanism for making such obligations a condition of finishing rather than a good intention.
questions.mindset: Write down what changed while changing it, because later never has the detail.

questions.stem: Leadership has decided, for cost reasons, that the next five developers on your agile team will be hired in Manila, seven hours ahead of your London office. The decision is final. Your team relies heavily on pairing and whiteboard discussions, and almost nothing about the reasons for its design choices is written down. The new developers start in six weeks. How should you approach knowledge sharing?

options.text: Shift part of the London day to create a daily overlap for pairing on the hardest areas, and start writing short decision records and recorded walkthroughs that Manila can use outside it.
options.rationale: It accepts the constraint and redesigns the practices around it. Scarce shared hours go on what can only be learned live, and the reasoning that currently lives in conversation is written down so it can be reached seven hours later.

options.text: Make a case to leadership for hiring the five developers in London after all, setting out the cost of losing pairing and whiteboard sessions across a seven-hour time difference.
options.rationale: The candidate reopens a decision that has been made and stated as final. The argument spends credibility and the six weeks of preparation time, and the team still has no plan for the day the new developers arrive.

options.text: Give the Manila developers well-defined, self-contained stories that need little context, keeping work on the core design with London until the newcomers have built up enough experience of the product.
options.rationale: The candidate protects the core by keeping the knowledge where it already is. The new developers never meet the work that would teach them the design, and the team settles into two tiers with all the context on one side.

options.text: Fly two London developers to Manila for the first month to pair in person, then return to the team's usual pairing and whiteboard practices once the visitors are back home.
options.rationale: A good start, but the candidate treats the change as a one-off induction. The time difference is permanent, so practices that depend on everyone being awake together stop working the day the visitors fly home.

questions.explanation: When a fixed constraint changes how a team can work together, its knowledge-sharing practices have to be redesigned around the constraint rather than defended against it or bridged for a few weeks. Distributed teams spend their limited shared time on what can only be learned live and move everything else into written or recorded forms that can be used asynchronously. The test is whether the arrangement still works in the third month, not the first.
questions.mindset: When the way people meet changes for good, change how knowledge moves to match it.

questions.stem: A data science group has built a demand-forecasting model for a grocery chain as a set of notebooks. Your agile team will put it into production and maintain it. In six weeks the data scientists move to a new pricing project, though they stay in the same building. The model's lead author says the notebooks 'explain themselves'. Which two actions should you take to transfer what your team needs?

options.text: Have one data scientist work inside your team for the first sprints of productionising, pairing with developers on the code that prepares the data and runs the model.
options.rationale: Working together on the real job transfers how the model behaves in a way no reading can, and it lets developers ask questions at the moment they arise rather than guessing them in advance.

options.text: Ask the data scientists to write down the model's assumptions, known weak spots and the conditions under which it should be retrained, then review them with your team.
options.rationale: Only the authors know where the model stops being trustworthy, and the notebooks show what the code does rather than when it will be wrong. Making those limits explicit is what lets your team maintain it after the authors have moved on.

options.text: Ask the data scientists to add detailed comments to every notebook cell before they move, so that your developers can trace each step of the model's logic on their own.
options.rationale: The candidate takes the author's word that the code explains itself and asks only for more of it. Comments describe each step, not the assumptions behind the whole or the signs that the model has gone stale.

options.text: Arrange a half-day session in which the data scientists walk your whole team through the model's design, with time set aside for questions at the end of the session.
options.rationale: The candidate relies on a one-off broadcast. Developers do not know what to ask until they are working on the code, and by then the session is over and the authors are busy elsewhere.

options.text: Have your developers rebuild the model from scratch in the team's production language, using the notebooks as a specification, so that they understand every part they will own.
options.rationale: The candidate confuses rebuilding with understanding. A rewrite risks quietly changing validated behaviour, takes far longer, and still leaves the authors' assumptions about the data undiscovered.

questions.explanation: When work moves between disciplines, the receivers need two kinds of knowledge: how the thing works, which transfers best by doing real work alongside its authors, and where it stops being valid, which only the authors hold and which has to be made explicit. Artefacts such as code show what is done but rarely why, or under what conditions it fails. A handoff that covers only the first leaves the receivers maintaining something they cannot judge.
questions.mindset: Ask the authors where their work breaks, because the work itself will not say.

questions.stem: Funding for the detailed design of a coastal desalination plant has been frozen for nine months pending a government spending review. The design is 45% complete, and the twelve-person team will be redeployed to other projects within two weeks. The sponsor expects the work to restart with mostly different people. Which two actions should the project manager take before the team disperses?

options.text: Have each design lead record the open questions, unverified assumptions and the reasons behind decisions not yet shown in the drawings, as a restart pack for their discipline.
options.rationale: Drawings record what has been decided, not why, and not what was still being worked out. That reasoning is the first thing to fade over nine months and the most expensive to rediscover, and it can be captured cheaply only while the people are still here.

options.text: Agree with the new line managers of the five design leads that each will be released for a short briefing with their successor when the design work restarts.
options.rationale: Not everything can be written down in two weeks. Securing a formal claim on the leads' time at restart keeps a route to the knowledge that the restart pack misses, and agreeing it now is far easier than finding them later.

options.text: Bring every drawing, calculation and model up to a consistent issued standard before the team leaves, so that the design package is complete at the point where work stopped.
options.rationale: The candidate spends the last two weeks polishing the formal record, which is the part least at risk. Partial drawings brought to issue standard still do not say why choices were made or what was left unresolved.

options.text: Run a full lessons-learned workshop with the whole team, so that what the project has learned so far is captured in the register before people move to other projects.
options.rationale: The candidate reaches for the closure tool. Lessons serve future projects; the restart team needs the state of this design and the reasoning behind it, which a lessons register is not built to hold.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to retain two senior designers part-time through the freeze, so that the knowledge stays with people who already hold it until the work starts again.
options.rationale: The candidate stores knowledge in people instead of transferring it. During a funding freeze the request is unlikely to be granted, and even if it is, the restart then depends on two individuals still being available in nine months.

questions.explanation: When work is suspended rather than closed, the knowledge most at risk is the reasoning and the unfinished threads: why choices were made, what was still uncertain, and what was about to be decided. Formal deliverables do not hold this, and it decays fastest once people disperse. The remedy is to capture it while the people are still together and to secure a formal route back to them for whatever cannot be captured.
questions.mindset: Before a team disperses, capture the reasoning that the deliverables leave out.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is rolling out a new case-management system to 600 probation officers across twelve offices over three months. The training budget covers full-day classroom sessions for only 60 people. The system changes how officers record risk assessments, and pilot users made most of their mistakes in their second and third weeks of live use, not on day one. Which two actions make the best use of the budget?

options.text: Train five officers from each office as super users, and agree with office managers that they have protected time to support colleagues during the first month of live use.
options.rationale: Sixty places cannot train 600 people, but they can create a local expert in every team. Protected time is what turns a trained officer into a source of help rather than one more busy colleague.

options.text: Place floor support in each office during the second and third weeks after its go-live, when pilot users made most of their mistakes, rather than concentrating it on day one.
options.rationale: The pilot shows when the need peaks, and it is not at launch. Putting help where people are struggling on real cases transfers the knowledge at the moment it can be used.

options.text: Run the classroom budget as short two-hour sessions instead of full days, so that around 240 officers attend and far more of the workforce hears the material in person.
options.rationale: The candidate maximises reach at the cost of depth. Two hours cannot cover a changed way of recording risk, and attendance on day one does nothing for the weeks when the pilot showed mistakes happen.

options.text: Replace classroom training with e-learning modules that all 600 officers complete before go-live, so that everyone receives the same content at little additional cost.
options.rationale: The candidate equates coverage with transfer. Front-loaded, one-way content reaches everyone before the moment of need and leaves no one to turn to in the second and third weeks.

options.text: Ask the sponsor for enough additional budget to give all 600 officers a full day of classroom training in the weeks before their own office goes live.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes more of the same instruction is the answer. The pilot evidence says the problem arises after go-live, so a larger budget spent before it buys the wrong thing at a higher price.

questions.explanation: Limited training effort goes furthest when it multiplies and when it arrives at the point of need. A network of trained local experts with time to help turns a small number of places into support for everyone, and evidence about when users actually struggle should decide when help is available. Front-loading instruction for as many people as possible feels thorough but spends the budget before the knowledge can be used.
questions.mindset: Put scarce help where it multiplies and when people actually need it.

questions.stem: On your two-year port terminal expansion, you have found three separate reasons why knowledge is not reaching the people who need it. Match each finding to the response most likely to remove it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A senior geotechnical engineer answers questions in person but will not write anything down, because she believes her specialist knowledge is what protects her role in a coming restructure.
Site teams say they would use lessons from earlier terminals, but a search of the repository returns hundreds of untagged documents and they give up after a few minutes.
A specialist subcontractor declines to share its temporary-works calculations with your team, citing intellectual property, although the port will need them for future maintenance.

options.text: Make her the named author and reviewer of the published geotechnical guidance, so that sharing builds her standing
options.rationale: Her reluctance is rational given what she believes. Tying her recognition to the shared guidance turns writing it down from a threat to her position into evidence of her value.

options.text: Curate the repository: tag lessons by discipline and asset type and retire duplicates, so a search returns a short relevant list
options.rationale: The teams want the knowledge; the barrier is the cost of finding it. Curation lowers that cost, which is the only thing standing between a willing reader and the lesson.

options.text: Ask the commercial team to establish what the subcontract allows to be shared and negotiate terms for the rest
options.rationale: An intellectual property objection is a contractual question with a contractual answer. Settling what is owed under the subcontract, and buying what is not, gives the port a right to the knowledge rather than a favour.

options.text: Run awareness sessions for the whole project team on why sharing knowledge matters and how it benefits future projects
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three barriers is a lack of awareness: each has a specific cause, in personal incentive, findability and contract, that a general message would leave in place.

questions.explanation: Knowledge stops flowing for different reasons, and each reason has its own remedy: an incentive problem needs a change in what sharing earns the person, a findability problem needs curation, and an ownership problem needs a contractual answer. Generic encouragement fails because it treats all three as a lack of goodwill. Name the barrier before choosing the response.
questions.mindset: Find out why knowledge is stuck before deciding how to move it.

questions.stem: Your organisation has nine agile teams building an online learning platform for universities. Three cross-team knowledge needs have come up this month. Match each need to the sharing format that suits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Testers embedded in six different teams each keep solving the same test-data problems on their own, and want a lasting way to share what they find.
Your team needs a small change to a library owned by another team, which has no capacity this quarter, and none of your developers has worked in that library before.
One team has found a build configuration that halves pipeline times, and every other team could adopt it in an afternoon once shown how.

options.text: A community of practice for testers that meets regularly across teams
options.rationale: A recurring problem shared by one discipline across teams needs a lasting forum owned by its practitioners. A community of practice gives the testers a standing place to pool solutions as new problems arise.

options.text: An inner-source contribution: your team makes the change and the owning team reviews it before merging
options.rationale: Making the change under the owners' review moves knowledge of the library to your developers through real work, while the owning team keeps control of its code at the cost of a review rather than a build.

options.text: A short recorded demonstration with a written how-to guide shared with all teams
options.rationale: A stable, self-contained technique that others can adopt quickly needs only a clear one-off broadcast. A recording and a written guide reach every team at once and remain available to later joiners.

options.text: A permanent cross-team architecture board that approves changes to shared practices
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three needs is a question of approval. A board adds a gate in front of sharing and slows exactly the flow of knowledge each situation calls for.

questions.explanation: The right format for sharing knowledge across teams depends on the shape of the need: an ongoing problem shared by one discipline calls for a standing community, a one-off technique calls for a broadcast that persists, and knowledge of someone else's system is best gained by working in it under its owners' review. Choosing one format for every need either over-engineers simple sharing or under-serves recurring problems.
questions.mindset: Fit the sharing format to whether the need is recurring, one-off or hands-on.

questions.stem: On your project to build a regional flood defence scheme, three pieces of knowledge have emerged this week. Complete each sentence with the record that will carry the knowledge to whoever needs to act on it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The embankment design assumes the local clay will meet the specified strength, but no samples have been tested yet. This should be recorded in
The team has found that the environmental regulator takes twelve weeks, not the six the organisation's planning guide states, to approve works beside rivers. This should be recorded in
A subcontractor's foreman has explained how to sequence pumping so that the existing wall is not undermined during the next stage of excavation. This should be captured in

options.text: the assumption log, with an owner and a date by which it must be confirmed
options.rationale: An untested premise that the design depends on needs an owner and a deadline for verification. The assumption log keeps it visible until it is confirmed or the design is changed, so nobody builds on it unknowingly.

options.text: the lessons learned register, so that it shapes the rest of this project and reaches later ones
options.rationale: A discovery that corrects the organisation's own planning guidance is a lesson: it changes how this project schedules approvals and should change how future projects do too.

options.text: the method statement for that stage of excavation, which the crew will work from
options.rationale: Practical know-how about how to do a task safely belongs in the document the people doing the task actually use. Filed anywhere else, it will not be in front of the crew when they start pumping.

options.text: the change log, as an amendment to the approved project baseline
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three alters the approved scope, schedule or cost baseline as it stands. Logging them as changes would misdescribe them and route them to people who do not need to act on them.

questions.explanation: Each record in a project exists to carry a particular kind of knowledge to the people who act on it: unverified premises to whoever must confirm them, lessons to this and future projects, and task know-how to the people doing the task. Knowledge filed in the wrong record is technically captured but practically lost, because it does not reach the person who needs it at the moment they need it.
questions.mindset: Record knowledge where the person who must act on it will actually look.

questions.stem: Since handover of a new fleet-maintenance scheduling system, a bus operator's depot staff raise about 60 queries a month to your project engineers, each taking 1.5 hours to answer. A two-day hands-on workshop of 7.5 hours a day, attended by 2 of your engineers and 8 depot staff, is expected to cut queries by 70%. Count every attendee's time as cost.

blanks.label: Engineer hours saved per month after the workshop
blanks.rationale: 70% of 60 queries is 42 queries a month avoided, and each takes 1.5 hours: 42 × 1.5 = 63 hours saved per month.

blanks.label: Total person-hours the workshop costs
blanks.rationale: Ten people attend (2 engineers + 8 depot staff) for two days of 7.5 hours, so 10 × 15 = 150 person-hours.

blanks.label: Months until the workshop has paid back its cost, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Payback is the one-off cost divided by the monthly saving: 150 ÷ 63 = 2.38, about 2.4 months. After that, each month saves a further 63 hours of engineering time.

questions.explanation: A continuing stream of questions after handover is a sign that knowledge has not transferred, and it carries a recurring cost that can be set against a one-off investment in transferring it properly. Counting the time of everyone who attends, not just the trainers, gives an honest payback figure. When the payback is short, the recurring support is the expensive option even though it never appears as a single decision.
questions.mindset: Price the questions you keep answering against the cost of teaching once.

questions.stem: Your agile team's knowledge map lists each component it owns, how many developers can change it safely, how often it has changed recently and who uses it. You can fund one pairing rotation next sprint. Select the component where spreading knowledge reduces the most risk.

graphic.title: Team knowledge map: five components with developer coverage, change frequency and users
graphic.caption: Select a component. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Card payment adapter — 1 developer can change it; changed in 9 of the last 10 sprints; customer-facing
regions.rationale: One person, constant change and customers depending on it: every factor that makes concentrated knowledge dangerous is present at once. A pairing rotation here removes the most exposure for the effort.

regions.label: Legacy CSV exporter — 1 developer; changed in 1 of the last 10 sprints; being retired next quarter
regions.rationale: Coverage is as thin as it gets, which is what draws the eye, but the component barely changes and will be gone within a quarter. Knowledge spread here would be thrown away almost at once.

regions.label: Search service — 2 developers; changed in 8 of the last 10 sprints; customer-facing
regions.rationale: Busy and customer-facing, but two people can already change it, so losing one does not stop the work. The candidate weighs activity and forgets coverage.

regions.label: Admin settings screen — 1 developer; changed in 2 of the last 10 sprints; internal staff only
regions.rationale: Single coverage is a real gap, but rare changes and internal users mean an absence would cause little harm. It belongs later in the queue, not first.

regions.label: Notification service — 4 developers; changed in 6 of the last 10 sprints; customer-facing
regions.rationale: Customer-facing and active, but four developers already share it. More pairing here would add little resilience to a component that is already well covered.

questions.explanation: Knowledge concentration is a risk in proportion to how few people hold it, how often the work needs doing and how much harm a gap would cause. Where effort to spread knowledge is limited, it goes first to the area where all three are high, and not to whatever has the thinnest coverage on paper. A component that rarely changes or is about to be retired can wait, however few people understand it.
questions.mindset: Spread knowledge first where few hold it, the work is frequent and a gap would hurt.
